title: Adolf Hitler
subtitle: How a failed painter took a nation to war and genocide

package.intro: Adolf Hitler was handed power legally in January 1933. Twelve years later, his regime had murdered six million Jews and Europe lay in ruins. This documentary tells how a failed art student from Austria rose to dictator, step by step, and how many people helped him on the way.
facts: Born 20 April 1889 in Braunau am Inn, Austria-Hungary
Rejected twice by the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts (1907 and 1908)
Beer Hall Putsch, 8–9 November 1923; served about nine months of a five-year sentence
Nazi vote rose from 2.6% (1928) to 37.3% (July 1932); never a majority in a free election
Appointed chancellor 30 January 1933; Enabling Act passed 23 March 1933
About six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust
Died by suicide in the Führerbunker, Berlin, 30 April 1945; Germany surrendered 8 May 1945
package.sources: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (Holocaust Encyclopedia), Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ian Kershaw's Hitler biography, Richard J. Evans's Third Reich trilogy.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: ADOLF HITLER
lines.sub: The failed painter who took a nation to war and genocide

lines: In the spring of 1945, Berlin was a ruin. Soviet artillery was falling on the government quarter, and fifteen metres underground, in a concrete bunker, the man who had started it all was running out of time.
Twelve years earlier, he had been handed power legally, by the president of a democracy.

lines.label: Jewish men, women and children murdered in the Holocaust

lines: In those twelve years, his regime murdered six million Jews.

lines.label: estimated deaths in the Second World War

lines: And it started a war in Europe that helped make the Second World War the deadliest conflict in human history.

lines.text: How did one man get there?

lines: Adolf Hitler is the name the world reaches for when it wants to describe evil. But he did not do it alone, and he did not do it all at once. This is how it happened.

sections.name: A failed artist
lines: Adolf Hitler was born on the twentieth of April, 1889, in Braunau am Inn, a small Austrian town on the border with Germany.

lines.name: Adolf Hitler
lines.role: Born in Austria. Wanted to be a painter.

lines: His father was a customs official with a temper. His mother, Klara, doted on him. As a teenager he drifted out of school and dreamed of becoming an artist.

lines.label: times rejected by the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts

lines: In 1907, and again in 1908, the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna turned him down. His mother died of cancer in between.
For the next five years he lived in Vienna on very little, at times in a men's hostel, selling small paintings of city scenes to get by.

lines.head: A city of hatreds
lines.sub: Pamphlets, rallies and a populist mayor

lines: Vienna was a city full of nationalist pamphlets and a mayor who used hatred of Jews to win votes. Hitler later claimed this was where his worldview formed.

sections.name: War and defeat
lines: In 1913 he moved to Munich. When war broke out the next year, he volunteered for the Bavarian army.

lines.name: Corporal Hitler
lines.role: Dispatch runner on the Western Front. Iron Cross, First Class.

lines: He served for four years as a regimental dispatch runner, carrying messages near the front lines, and was awarded the Iron Cross.
In October 1918 he was temporarily blinded in a gas attack. He was in a hospital bed when he heard that Germany had surrendered.

The peace treaty that followed took territory from Germany, limited its army, and demanded huge reparations. Many Germans believed a lie: that their army had not really lost, but had been stabbed in the back by traitors at home. Hitler believed it, and he blamed Jews and communists.

sections.name: The rise
lines: Back in Munich, the army sent him to watch a tiny political group called the German Workers' Party. He joined it instead. He discovered he had one great talent. He could hold a crowd.

lines.name: Party leader
lines.role: Leader of the National Socialist German Workers' Party: the Nazis.

lines: The party renamed itself the National Socialist German Workers' Party, the Nazis. By 1921, Hitler was its leader.
In November 1923, he tried to seize power by force in Munich. The coup collapsed in a single day. Sixteen of his followers and four police officers were killed.
He was convicted of treason and sentenced to five years. He served about nine months, in comfortable conditions, and used the time to dictate a book: Mein Kampf, My Struggle.

lines.text: Mein Kampf laid it all out: racial struggle, conquest of land in the east, and the Jews cast as the enemy.

lines: The book set out almost everything he would later try to do. A world of racial struggle. Conquest of living space in the east. And Jews cast as the enemy behind every problem.

lines.text: He decided to take power through the ballot box.

lines: When he got out, he changed tactics. He would not storm power again. He would win it through elections.

sections.name: Taking power
lines: In 1928 the Nazis won less than three percent of the vote. Then came the Great Depression. Millions of Germans lost their jobs, and the extremes grew.

lines.label: July 1932 · largest party in the Reichstag

lines: By July 1932, the Nazis were the largest party in parliament, with about thirty-seven percent. They never won a majority in a free election.
Conservative politicians believed they could use him and control him. On the thirtieth of January 1933, President Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor.
Four weeks later, the parliament building burned. Hitler used the fire as a pretext. Civil liberties were suspended, and thousands of political opponents were arrested.
In March, the Enabling Act let his government make laws without parliament. Within months, every other party was banned.

lines.label: Night of the Long Knives · June 1934

lines: In the summer of 1934, he had rivals inside his own movement murdered, along with old enemies. When Hindenburg died that August, Hitler merged the offices of president and chancellor. He was now the Führer, and the army swore an oath to him personally.

sections.name: Persecution
lines: Persecution began at once and grew step by step. Jews were pushed out of jobs. In 1935, the Nuremberg Laws stripped them of citizenship.
In November 1938, on Kristallnacht, synagogues were burned and Jewish shops smashed across the country. Around thirty thousand Jewish men were sent to concentration camps.
All the while, a propaganda machine told Germans that their Führer had restored jobs, pride and order. Many believed it.

sections.name: War
lines: Next came expansion. Austria was annexed in March 1938. That September, Britain and France agreed at Munich to let him take part of Czechoslovakia, hoping to keep the peace.
It did not work. On the first of September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Two days later, Britain and France declared war.
Within two years, his armies had conquered most of Europe, from France to Greece. In June 1941, he invaded the Soviet Union.

lines.head: Germany declares war on the United States

lines: And in December 1941, after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, he declared war on the United States as well.

sections.name: The Holocaust
lines: Behind the front lines, the regime carried out the systematic murder of Europe's Jews.
Mobile killing squads shot more than a million people in the occupied east. Then came the death camps: Auschwitz, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno, Majdanek.
In January 1942, senior officials met at a villa at Wannsee, near Berlin, to coordinate what they called the Final Solution.

lines.label: about two in three of Europe's Jews were murdered

lines: About six million Jews were murdered. Roughly two out of every three Jews living in Europe.
Hundreds of thousands of Roma, disabled people, political prisoners and others were also killed, along with millions of Soviet prisoners of war.

sections.name: The fall
lines: The tide turned at Stalingrad, where an entire German army surrendered in February 1943.

lines.name: 20 July 1944
lines.role: An officer's bomb exploded under the map table. Hitler survived.

lines: In July 1944, an officer, Claus von Stauffenberg, planted a bomb at his headquarters. It went off, but Hitler survived. Thousands of suspects were arrested and around two hundred were executed.
By April 1945, Soviet troops were fighting in the streets of Berlin. Hitler refused to surrender and blamed the German people for failing him.
On the twenty-ninth of April, he married his long-time companion, Eva Braun. The next afternoon, they both took their own lives.
Eight days later, Germany surrendered unconditionally.

sections.name: Legacy
lines: At Nuremberg, the surviving leaders of his regime were put on trial before an international court. It helped establish that crimes against humanity could be prosecuted.
In 1948, the United Nations adopted the Genocide Convention. Germany, over decades, confronted what had been done in its name.

The hardest lesson of Hitler's story is not that one evil man rose to power. It is how many ordinary people, institutions and politicians helped him get there, believing at each step that it would not go further.
It did go further. That is why the world still says his name, and why it still says: never again.
